newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - March 6.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - March 6.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Thursday:

* Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's soothing remarks, in which he said the U.S. stock market would be overvalued only if analysts' projections for higher earnings prove wrong in coming years, sent the Dow industrials up 93.13 to close at 6,945.85.

* Although growth stocks have been lagging, analysts are keen about a new index, the Montgomery Securities Growth Stock Index, which is based on the 500 stocks for which Wall Street expects the greatest profit growth in the coming years.

* H. Wayne Huizenga is seeking to make an empire out of auto retailer Republic Industries in much the same way he pursued industry consolidations for Waste Management Inc and Blockbuster Entertainment.

* Federal district Judge Robert Sweet plans to impose an unusually severe penalty on New York financier Steven Hoffenberg, who is accused of masterminding the biggest financial swindle in U.S. history as the former head of Towers Financial Corp.
* The 30-year bond yield fell to 6.82 percent from 6.86.

* Economist Dean Baker of the Economic Policy Institute says the rise of the stock market cannot be sustained, contending that the 7 percent real return over the last 70 years is incompatible with forecasts of economic growth of less than 2 percent over the long haul.
* The share price of Broderbund Software dropped after the company sald its second quarter earnings would fall below analysts' estimates.
* Kmart said its quarterly net loss narrowed and that results from continuing operations swung into the black.
* Donna Karan and Designer Holdings ended a six-month pact calling for Designer Holdings to make jeans for Donna Karan.
* Omnicom is expanding in health care advertising with an agreement to buy Cline, Davis & Mann, a New York company with billings estimated at $170 million.
* The Swiss government proposed creating a $4.7 billion fund to help victims of the Holocaust and other calamities.
* The family of Reginald Lewis, the former chairman of TLC Beatrice, has tentatively agreed to return about $15 million to settle a lawsuit brought by the company.
* The German economy grew unexpectedly in the fourth quarter at a rate of one-tenth of 1 percent.

* After Cuban-made pajamas were found in the stores of its Canadian subsidiary, Wal-Mart finds itself caught between the U.S.'s Helms-Burton Act and a Canadian law that bars companies operating in Canada from obeying U.S. laws that try to further the U.S. trade embargo against Cuba.
* A Federal judge began hearing arguments on whether Toys R Us illegally colluded with manufacturers to inflate toy prices.
* New York city's unemployment rate rose to 9.9 percent in January, the highest monthly level in nearly three years.
